opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most underappreciated ideas in the AlphaGo lineage, and it's something I spent a lot of time playing with myself. The core trick is that MCTS acts as a policy improvement operator. You take your current network, you run search on top of it, and the visit distribution that comes out of the search is just a better policy than the raw network prior. Then you distill that improved distribution back into the network. So search is the teacher and the network is the student, and they bootstrap each other.

What I find really interesting is what happens when you apply that relabeling to past experience rather than only fresh self-play. You have this big buffer of positions, maybe from old games, maybe from weaker versions of the model, and instead of trusting the actions that were actually played, you go back and rerun search with your current, stronger network and relabel each position with the new search targets. In a sense it's like hindsight: the data was collected by a dumb policy, but you get to annotate it with what a smarter policy would have done. That decouples data collection from label quality, which is a really nice property because collecting games is expensive and compute for relabeling is comparatively cheap.

There are some caveats, though. One is distribution shift. The states in your old buffer were visited by an older policy, so you're getting supervision on positions your current policy might never reach, and you're under-covering the positions it does reach. In Go that's somewhat forgiving because the state space is so rich and positions transfer reasonably well, but you can't totally get rid of on-policy play. The other is that the value targets are trickier than the policy targets. Relabeling the policy with search visit counts is pretty clean, but the game outcome was produced by the old policy, so if you use that as the value target you're baking in stale information. You either need to re-estimate value with search too, or accept some bias.

The bigger reason I like it is what it says beyond Go. A lot of people think of AlphaZero as "RL," but if you squint, the training loop is mostly supervised learning on labels produced by a more expensive computation. That's a really general recipe: spend inference-time compute to generate better labels, then amortize it into the weights. You see the same pattern now with language models, where you sample, verify or search, and then fine-tune on the improved outputs. So for me the MCTS relabeler is almost the cleanest toy example of that whole philosophy. It works really well in Go because you have a perfect simulator and a crisp reward, and the open question is how much of that carries over when your "search" is noisier and your verifier isn't perfect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really interesting, because it sits right at the intersection of two ideas that I think are underappreciated: hindsight relabeling and search as a learning signal.

Let me set it up. In standard AlphaZero-style training, you run MCTS at each position, the search produces an improved policy, and you distill that improved policy back into the network. The search is kind of acting as a policy improvement operator. What you're describing, using MCTS as a relabeler on past experience, is a slightly different framing. You take trajectories you've already collected, maybe from an older policy, maybe from human games, maybe from random play, and you go back and re-run search on those states to produce better targets than whatever the original actor actually did.

The thing I like about that is it's basically hindsight relabeling, but with a much stronger teacher. In goal-conditioned RL, hindsight experience replay says "whatever you ended up doing, pretend that was the goal." Here you're saying "whatever you did, let me use compute to figure out what you should have done, and train on that instead." You're decoupling the data collection policy from the quality of the training signal. That's really nice from a data efficiency standpoint, because Go games are expensive to play but the states in them are reusable. You don't have to throw away old experience just because the policy that generated it was bad.

There are a few caveats I'd flag, though. The first is distribution shift. If your old trajectories are from a weak policy, you're relabeling states that a strong policy would never visit. You can spend a lot of search compute getting really good labels for positions that don't matter. So there's a question of how much of your compute budget goes to relabeling the replay buffer versus generating fresh on-policy games. My intuition is you want some mix, and the right mix probably changes over training.

The second thing is that MCTS targets are only as good as the value function driving the search. Early on, your value net is bad, so the relabeled policy is sort of bootstrapping off garbage. It still helps, because search amplifies even a mediocre prior, but it means the relabeled targets aren't ground truth, they're just a better estimate. You have to be a bit careful not to treat them as fixed supervised labels forever. You probably want to re-relabel as the value function improves, which is more compute again.

And the third, which is more of a conceptual point, is that Go is almost the best possible case for this. You have a perfect simulator, deterministic dynamics, cheap state copies. The reason this is attractive in Go is precisely the reason it's hard to apply elsewhere. In robotics, which is where I spend most of my time, you don't get to rewind the world and run search from an arbitrary past state. So I look at this and think, the real question is what's the analog when you don't have a simulator. Maybe it's a learned world model, maybe it's a language model doing some kind of reasoning over the trajectory. But the pattern of "collect cheap experience, spend compute later to upgrade the labels" is, I think, going to be a big deal across the board, and Go is a clean place to study it.

So overall I'd say it's a good idea, it's well-motivated, and the main things to watch are where you're spending search compute and how stale the relabels get as the value function moves.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a compelling way to turn additional computation into a better training signal. You take a position from a past game, run MCTS with your current model, and use the search’s action distribution as a new target for the policy. Even though the position is old, your assessment of what you should have done can improve.

The interesting thing is that you’re not just imitating the move you happened to play, or reinforcing it because you eventually won. You’re asking, “Given what I know now, what would I do here?” Then you distill that more expensive deliberation into a policy that can act cheaply.

The caveat is that search still depends on the quality of your policy and value estimates. More search doesn’t automatically produce a correct label. And relabeling old positions doesn’t replace collecting new experience, because an improved policy will encounter different positions. But in Go, where you have exact rules and can simulate consequences, it’s a very natural way to reuse experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a powerful idea because your past experience isn’t necessarily labeled with the best action you could have taken. It’s labeled with the action your policy happened to take at the time. With MCTS, you can revisit that position, spend more compute thinking about it, and produce a better training target.

Then you distill that search back into the policy. You’re teaching a relatively cheap network to approximate the result of a more expensive computation. As the policy and value function improve, the search can improve, and that gives you another round of better targets.

The caveat is that the relabeler isn’t an oracle. If your value estimates are systematically wrong, search can reinforce those errors. And there’s a compute allocation question: how much should you spend reanalyzing old positions versus generating new experience? But Go is a particularly good setting for this because you have the rules and can simulate alternative moves exactly.
